question: What are the six common stages of the data science pipeline described in the notes?
gold_answers: problem framing, data collection, data cleaning, exploratory analysis, modeling or summarization, and communication
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: The data science pipeline is a repeatable sequence of stages used to turn raw observations into decision-ready insights. A common educational framing lists six stages: problem framing, data collection, data cleaning, exploratory analysis, modeling or summarization, and communication of results.

reference_answer: problem framing, data collection, data cleaning, exploratory analysis, modeling or summarization, and communication

question: Why should problem framing happen before modeling begins?
gold_answers: to avoid optimizing the wrong metric or answering an irrelevant question
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: Problem framing defines the decision or scientific question before any modeling begins. Without a clear framing statement, later stages risk optimizing the wrong metric or answering an irrelevant question.

reference_answer: to avoid optimizing the wrong metric or answering an irrelevant question

question: What should a data collection plan record according to the lecture notes?
gold_answers: sampling design, time window, and known coverage gaps
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: Data collection gathers observations from sensors, surveys, logs, databases, or public repositories. The collection plan should record sampling design, time window, and known coverage gaps so that later analysts can judge external validity.

reference_answer: sampling design, time window, and known coverage gaps

question: Why should data cleaning decisions be logged?
gold_answers: because they change the effective sample and can bias downstream estimates
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: Data cleaning handles missing values, inconsistent encodings, duplicate rows, and obvious sensor errors. Cleaning decisions should be logged because they change the effective sample and can bias downstream estimates.

reference_answer: because they change the effective sample and can bias downstream estimates

question: What is exploratory data analysis intended to generate before formal modeling?
gold_answers: hypotheses and quality checks
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) uses summaries and visualizations to understand distributions, correlations, and anomalies before formal modeling. EDA is intended to generate hypotheses and quality checks, not to replace confirmatory analysis.

reference_answer: hypotheses and quality checks

question: What must a complete communication package state?
gold_answers: assumptions, uncertainty, and what the analysis cannot claim
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: Communication translates analytical findings into stakeholder language using tables, charts, and limitations. A complete communication package states assumptions, uncertainty, and what the analysis cannot claim.

reference_answer: assumptions, uncertainty, and what the analysis cannot claim

question: How are numerical variables commonly classified in introductory data science?
gold_answers: continuous or discrete
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: In introductory data science, variables are commonly classified as numerical or categorical. Numerical variables take quantitative values and may be continuous (any value in an interval) or discrete (countable integers).

reference_answer: continuous or discrete

question: What is the difference between nominal and ordinal categorical variables?
gold_answers: nominal categories have no intrinsic order; ordinal categories have a meaningful order
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: Categorical variables take a limited set of labels. Nominal categories have no intrinsic order (for example, browser type), whereas ordinal categories have a meaningful order (for example, Likert agreement levels).

reference_answer: nominal categories have no intrinsic order; ordinal categories have a meaningful order

question: What does a tidy data table store in each column, row, and table?
gold_answers: each variable in a column, each observation in a row, and each type of observational unit in its own table
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: A tidy data table stores each variable in a column, each observation in a row, and each type of observational unit in its own table. Tidy structure simplifies joins, filters, and group-wise summaries.

reference_answer: each variable in a column, each observation in a row, and each type of observational unit in its own table

question: Why must a held-out test set remain untouched during model fitting?
gold_answers: so that reported performance estimates remain honest
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: Train-test separation keeps a held-out test set untouched during model fitting so that reported performance estimates remain honest. Using test labels during feature selection or threshold tuning produces overly optimistic scores.

reference_answer: so that reported performance estimates remain honest

question: What artifacts does reproducibility require recording?
gold_answers: code versions, random seeds, package versions, and the exact dataset snapshot
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: Reproducibility requires recording code versions, random seeds, package versions, and the exact dataset snapshot used for a reported result. Without those artifacts, later auditors cannot regenerate the same numbers.

reference_answer: code versions, random seeds, package versions, and the exact dataset snapshot

question: Which plot types are commonly used for numerical, categorical, and pairwise numerical relationships in EDA?
gold_answers: histograms, bar charts, and scatter plots
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: Exploratory plots commonly include histograms for single numerical variables, bar charts for categorical frequencies, and scatter plots for pairwise numerical relationships. Plot choice should match the variable types involved.

reference_answer: histograms, bar charts, and scatter plots

question: What are three commonly summarized missingness mechanisms?
gold_answers: MCAR, MAR, and MNAR
missing completely at random, missing at random, or missing not at random
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: Missingness mechanisms are often summarized as missing completely at random (MCAR), missing at random (MAR), or missing not at random (MNAR). The mechanism affects whether simple deletion or imputation is defensible.

reference_answer: MCAR, MAR, and MNAR

question: Does a correlation coefficient by itself prove causation?
gold_answers: no
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: A correlation coefficient summarizes linear association between two numerical variables but does not by itself prove causation. Confounding variables can induce strong correlations between unrelated quantities.

reference_answer: no

question: What can large imbalances in a cross-tabulation reveal?
gold_answers: sampling bias or a rare class
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: Cross-tabulation counts how categorical variables co-occur. Large imbalances in a cross-tab can reveal sampling bias or a rare class that will challenge classification models.

reference_answer: sampling bias or a rare class

question: What ethical principles does educational data science ethics emphasize?
gold_answers: informed consent, purpose limitation, and minimization of collected personal attributes
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: Educational data science ethics emphasizes informed consent, purpose limitation, and minimization of collected personal attributes. Collecting more fields than needed increases privacy risk without improving the stated analysis goal.

reference_answer: informed consent, purpose limitation, and minimization of collected personal attributes

question: How can postal code act as a proxy variable?
gold_answers: it may correlate with protected class membership and recreate discriminatory patterns
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: Proxy variables can encode sensitive attributes indirectly. For example, postal code may correlate with protected class membership and can recreate discriminatory patterns even when the sensitive attribute is removed.

reference_answer: it may correlate with protected class membership and recreate discriminatory patterns

question: Why can a single aggregate accuracy number be misleading for fairness?
gold_answers: it can hide large group disparities
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: Fairness checks compare error rates or selection rates across demographic groups when such attributes are available for auditing. A single aggregate accuracy number can hide large group disparities.

reference_answer: it can hide large group disparities

question: What do data retention policies specify?
gold_answers: how long raw and derived records are stored and when they must be deleted or anonymized
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: Data retention policies specify how long raw and derived records are stored and when they must be deleted or anonymized. Indefinite retention increases breach impact and conflicts with purpose limitation.

reference_answer: how long raw and derived records are stored and when they must be deleted or anonymized

question: In high-stakes settings, what role should the model play relative to human oversight?
gold_answers: the model advises; institutional policy determines who may act
title: data_science

evidence_spans.text: Human oversight keeps a qualified reviewer responsible for high-stakes decisions supported by models. The model advises; institutional policy determines who may act on the advice.

reference_answer: the model advises; institutional policy determines who may act

question: What do descriptive statistics summarize without drawing formal inferences about a population?
gold_answers: a sample
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: Descriptive statistics summarize a sample without drawing formal inferences about a larger population. Common numerical summaries include the mean, median, mode, variance, and standard deviation.

reference_answer: a sample

question: Why is the mean sensitive to extreme values?
gold_answers: because extreme values pull the average
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: The arithmetic mean is the sum of observations divided by the count of observations. The mean is sensitive to extreme values, so skewed distributions are often also summarized with the median.

reference_answer: because extreme values pull the average

question: How is the median defined for an even number of observations?
gold_answers: the average of the two central values
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: The median is the middle value after sorting the sample. For an even number of observations, the median is typically the average of the two central values.

reference_answer: the average of the two central values

question: What is the sample standard deviation in relation to the sample variance?
gold_answers: the square root of the sample variance
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: Variance measures average squared deviation from the mean. The sample standard deviation is the square root of the sample variance and is expressed in the same units as the original variable.

reference_answer: the square root of the sample variance

question: What is the interquartile range (IQR)?
gold_answers: the distance between the 75th and 25th percentiles
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: A percentile is a value below which a given percentage of observations fall. The interquartile range (IQR) is the distance between the 75th and 25th percentiles and summarizes spread with reduced sensitivity to extremes.

reference_answer: the distance between the 75th and 25th percentiles

question: How are relative frequencies computed from frequency counts?
gold_answers: divide counts by the sample size
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: A frequency distribution counts how often values or bins occur. Relative frequencies divide those counts by the sample size so that comparisons across differently sized samples remain meaningful.

reference_answer: divide counts by the sample size

question: What is a point estimate?
gold_answers: a single number approximating a population parameter
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: Inferential statistics use sample data to make probabilistic statements about a population parameter. A point estimate is a single number approximating the parameter; an interval estimate gives a range of plausible values.

reference_answer: a single number approximating a population parameter

question: What is the standard error?
gold_answers: the standard deviation of the sampling distribution
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: A sampling distribution describes how a statistic varies across repeated random samples of the same size from the same population. The standard error is the standard deviation of that sampling distribution.

reference_answer: the standard deviation of the sampling distribution

question: What does the central limit theorem say about the sampling distribution of the sample mean for large n?
gold_answers: it is approximately normal even when the population is not normal, under mild conditions
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: The central limit theorem states that, for sufficiently large sample size, the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal even when the population distribution is not normal, under mild conditions.

reference_answer: it is approximately normal even when the population is not normal, under mild conditions

question: What does a 95 percent confidence level represent in introductory teaching?
gold_answers: a common educational default, not a universal requirement
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: A confidence interval for a mean combines a point estimate with a margin of error based on the standard error and a critical value from a reference distribution. A 95 percent confidence level is a common educational default, not a universal requirement.

reference_answer: a common educational default, not a universal requirement

question: What is bias of an estimator?
gold_answers: the difference between the expected value of the estimator and the true parameter
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: Bias of an estimator is the difference between the expected value of the estimator and the true parameter. Unbiasedness does not guarantee small variance; mean squared error combines bias and variance.

reference_answer: the difference between the expected value of the estimator and the true parameter

question: What property does simple random sampling give equally sized subsets?
gold_answers: the same chance of selection
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: Simple random sampling gives every equally sized subset of the population the same chance of selection. Convenience samples lack that design property and generally do not support classical frequentist coverage claims.

reference_answer: the same chance of selection

question: What does the null hypothesis typically state?
gold_answers: a baseline claim about a parameter, often of no effect or no difference
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: A null hypothesis states a baseline claim about a parameter, often of no effect or no difference. The alternative hypothesis states the claim the study seeks evidence for.

reference_answer: a baseline claim about a parameter, often of no effect or no difference

question: What is a p-value?
gold_answers: the probability, under the null hypothesis, of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: A p-value is the probability, under the null hypothesis, of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. A small p-value indicates incompatibility between the data and the null model, not the probability that the null is true.

reference_answer: the probability, under the null hypothesis, of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed

question: What is a Type I error?
gold_answers: rejecting a true null hypothesis
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: The significance level alpha is a prechosen threshold for Type I error, the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis. Comparing the p-value to alpha is one rule for a binary reject / fail-to-reject decision.

reference_answer: rejecting a true null hypothesis

question: What is statistical power?
gold_answers: one minus the Type II error probability
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: A Type II error fails to reject a false null hypothesis. Statistical power is one minus the Type II error probability and increases with sample size, effect size, and reduced noise.

reference_answer: one minus the Type II error probability

question: In simple linear regression, what does the slope coefficient describe?
gold_answers: the expected change in the response for a one-unit increase in the predictor
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: Simple linear regression models a response variable as a linear function of one predictor plus an error term. The slope coefficient describes the expected change in the response for a one-unit increase in the predictor.

reference_answer: the expected change in the response for a one-unit increase in the predictor

question: What does ordinary least squares minimize?
gold_answers: the sum of squared residuals
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: Ordinary least squares chooses the intercept and slope that minimize the sum of squared residuals. Residuals are observed responses minus fitted values.

reference_answer: the sum of squared residuals

question: Does high R-squared prove that a regression model is causal?
gold_answers: no
title: statistics

evidence_spans.text: R-squared measures the proportion of variance in the response explained by the fitted model. High R-squared does not prove that the model is correctly specified or causal.

reference_answer: no

question: Why is extrapolating far outside the observed predictor range unreliable?
gold_answers: the fitted linear relationship may not continue

question: What does supervised learning require in the training examples?
gold_answers: input features and a known target label
title: machine_learning

evidence_spans.text: Supervised learning trains a model on examples that include both input features and a known target label. The fitted model is then used to predict labels for new unlabeled inputs.

reference_answer: input features and a known target label

question: What is the difference between classification and regression in machine learning?
gold_answers: classification predicts a discrete class label; regression predicts a continuous numeric target
title: machine_learning

evidence_spans.text: Classification predicts a discrete class label, such as spam versus not spam. Regression in the machine-learning sense predicts a continuous numeric target.

reference_answer: classification predicts a discrete class label; regression predicts a continuous numeric target

question: What are the roles of training, validation, and test sets?
gold_answers: training fits parameters; validation compares models or hyperparameters; test gives a final unbiased estimate
title: machine_learning

evidence_spans.text: A training set is used to fit parameters. A validation set is used to compare candidate models or hyperparameters. A test set is used once for a final unbiased performance estimate.

reference_answer: training fits parameters; validation compares models or hyperparameters; test gives a final unbiased estimate

question: What is overfitting?
gold_answers: when a model captures noise or idiosyncrasies of the training sample and generalizes poorly
title: machine_learning

evidence_spans.text: Overfitting occurs when a model captures noise or idiosyncrasies of the training sample and then generalizes poorly to new data. Underfitting occurs when the model is too simple to capture the systematic pattern.

reference_answer: when a model captures noise or idiosyncrasies of the training sample and generalizes poorly

question: What does k-fold cross-validation do?
gold_answers: partitions training data so each fold serves once as a temporary validation set
title: machine_learning

evidence_spans.text: Cross-validation partitions the training data into folds so that each fold serves once as a temporary validation set. k-fold cross-validation is a standard educational procedure for estimating generalization under data scarcity.

reference_answer: partitions training data so each fold serves once as a temporary validation set

question: Why is feature scaling used for many distance-based methods?

question: What is precision?

question: What is recall?
gold_answers: the fraction of truly positive cases that the model correctly identifies
title: machine_learning

gold_answers: true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives

question: How is data mining characterized in the introductory notes?
gold_answers: extracting previously unknown, potentially useful patterns from large datasets
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: Data mining extracts previously unknown, potentially useful patterns from large datasets. It sits at the intersection of databases, statistics, and machine learning, with emphasis on scalable pattern discovery.

reference_answer: extracting previously unknown, potentially useful patterns from large datasets

question: What stages does the KDD process typically include?
gold_answers: selection, preprocessing, transformation, data mining, and interpretation or evaluation
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: The knowledge discovery in databases (KDD) process typically includes selection, preprocessing, transformation, data mining, and interpretation or evaluation of patterns. Mining is one stage inside a broader discovery workflow.

reference_answer: selection, preprocessing, transformation, data mining, and interpretation or evaluation

question: What is the difference between descriptive and predictive data mining?
gold_answers: descriptive summarizes patterns such as associations or clusters; predictive forecasts unknown values or future events
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: Descriptive data mining summarizes data through patterns such as associations or clusters. Predictive data mining builds models that forecast unknown values or future events.

reference_answer: descriptive summarizes patterns such as associations or clusters; predictive forecasts unknown values or future events

question: What criteria can make a pattern interesting?
gold_answers: support, confidence, novelty, and actionability
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: Pattern interestingness depends on criteria such as support, confidence, novelty, and actionability. A statistically frequent pattern may still be uninteresting if it is obvious to domain experts.

reference_answer: support, confidence, novelty, and actionability

question: What is association rule mining looking for?
gold_answers: implications of the form antecedent implies consequent in transactional data
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: Association rule mining finds implications of the form antecedent implies consequent in transactional data. A classic educational example is market-basket analysis of items purchased together.

reference_answer: implications of the form antecedent implies consequent in transactional data

question: What is support of an itemset?
gold_answers: the fraction of transactions that contain all items in the set
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: Support of an itemset is the fraction of transactions that contain all items in the set. Minimum support filters out rare itemsets before rules are formed.

reference_answer: the fraction of transactions that contain all items in the set

question: How is confidence of a rule X implies Y defined?
gold_answers: support of X union Y divided by support of X
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: Confidence of a rule X implies Y is the support of X union Y divided by the support of X. Confidence estimates how often Y appears among transactions that contain X.

reference_answer: support of X union Y divided by support of X

question: What does lift greater than one suggest?
gold_answers: a positive association beyond chance co-occurrence under independence
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: Lift compares a rule's confidence to the baseline frequency of the consequent. Lift greater than one suggests a positive association beyond chance co-occurrence under independence.

reference_answer: a positive association beyond chance co-occurrence under independence

question: What does the Apriori principle state?
gold_answers: all subsets of a frequent itemset must themselves be frequent
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: The Apriori principle states that all subsets of a frequent itemset must themselves be frequent. Apriori uses this monotonicity to prune the candidate search space.

reference_answer: all subsets of a frequent itemset must themselves be frequent

question: Are association rules causal statements?
gold_answers: no
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: Association rules are not causal statements. A strong rule can reflect confounding, store layout, or marketing bundles rather than a mechanism that forces the consequent.

reference_answer: no

question: What does agglomerative hierarchical clustering do?
gold_answers: starts with each point alone and merges closest clusters until a stopping rule is met
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of merges or splits. Agglomerative hierarchical clustering starts with each point alone and merges closest clusters until a stopping rule is met.

reference_answer: starts with each point alone and merges closest clusters until a stopping rule is met

question: What does cutting a dendrogram at a height yield?
gold_answers: a flat partition with a chosen number of clusters
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: A dendrogram visualizes hierarchical merges. Cutting the dendrogram at a height yields a flat partition with a chosen number of clusters.

reference_answer: a flat partition with a chosen number of clusters

question: How does DBSCAN differ from k-means regarding the number of clusters?
gold_answers: DBSCAN does not require specifying the number of clusters in advance
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: Density-based methods such as DBSCAN group points in dense regions and can label sparse points as noise. Unlike k-means, DBSCAN does not require specifying the number of clusters in advance.

reference_answer: DBSCAN does not require specifying the number of clusters in advance

question: What does the silhouette score measure?
gold_answers: how similar a point is to its own cluster compared with the nearest other cluster
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: The silhouette score measures how similar a point is to its own cluster compared with the nearest other cluster. Average silhouette width is often used to compare candidate values of k.

reference_answer: how similar a point is to its own cluster compared with the nearest other cluster

question: Why should evaluation compare partitions rather than raw cluster label integers?
gold_answers: cluster labels are arbitrary identifiers
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: Cluster labels are arbitrary identifiers. Two runs can discover the same partition with permuted label numbers; evaluation should compare partitions, not raw label integers.

reference_answer: cluster labels are arbitrary identifiers

question: What are the phases of CRISP-DM?
gold_answers: business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, modeling, evaluation, and deployment
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: CRISP-DM is a widely taught process model for data mining projects. Its phases are business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, modeling, evaluation, and deployment.

reference_answer: business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, modeling, evaluation, and deployment

question: What does the business understanding phase translate organizational goals into?

question: What does evaluation in CRISP-DM judge beyond offline metrics?
gold_answers: whether the model meets business success criteria
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: Evaluation in CRISP-DM judges whether the model meets business success criteria, not only offline metric thresholds. A high F1 score can still fail if the operating cost of errors is unacceptable.

reference_answer: whether the model meets business success criteria

question: What does deployment integrate a model into?
gold_answers: an operational workflow with monitoring for performance drift
title: data_mining

evidence_spans.text: Deployment integrates a model into an operational workflow with monitoring for performance drift. Educational projects often stop at evaluation, but deployment is required for real impact.

question: What is the sample space of a random experiment?
gold_answers: the set of all possible outcomes
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: Probability quantifies uncertainty for random experiments with well-defined outcomes. The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of the experiment.

reference_answer: the set of all possible outcomes

question: What probability does the entire sample space have under a complete model?
gold_answers: one
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: An event is a subset of the sample space. The probability of an event is a number between zero and one inclusive, with the entire sample space having probability one under a complete model.

reference_answer: one

question: When are two events mutually exclusive?
gold_answers: if they cannot occur together / their intersection is empty
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot occur together, that is, their intersection is empty. For mutually exclusive events, the probability of their union equals the sum of their probabilities.

reference_answer: if they cannot occur together / their intersection is empty

question: What does the complement rule state?
gold_answers: the probability of an event not occurring equals one minus the probability that it occurs
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: The complement rule states that the probability of an event not occurring equals one minus the probability that it occurs. Complements are useful when the complementary event is easier to count.

reference_answer: the probability of an event not occurring equals one minus the probability that it occurs

question: Under a uniform finite model, how are event probabilities computed?
gold_answers: favorable counts divided by the size of the sample space
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: A uniform probability model on a finite sample space assigns equal probability to each outcome. Under uniformity, event probabilities reduce to favorable counts divided by the size of the sample space.

reference_answer: favorable counts divided by the size of the sample space

question: For independent events A and B, what equals P(A and B)?
gold_answers: P(A) times P(B)
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: Independence of two events means that the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other. For independent events A and B, P(A and B) equals P(A) times P(B).

reference_answer: P(A) times P(B)

question: What must a probability mass function sum to?
gold_answers: one
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: A discrete random variable takes a countable set of values, each with a probability mass. The probability mass function (PMF) assigns those probabilities and must sum to one.

reference_answer: one

question: For a continuous random variable with a density, what is the probability of any single exact point?
gold_answers: zero
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: A continuous random variable is described by a probability density function (PDF). Probabilities for continuous variables are areas under the PDF over intervals; the probability of any single exact point is zero under a continuous density.

reference_answer: zero

question: How is the expected value of a discrete random variable computed?
gold_answers: the sum of each value times its probability
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: The expected value of a discrete random variable is the sum of each value times its probability. For a continuous variable, the expectation is an integral of value times density.

reference_answer: the sum of each value times its probability

question: What does the Bernoulli distribution model?
gold_answers: a single success/failure trial with success probability p
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: The Bernoulli distribution models a single success/failure trial with success probability p. The binomial distribution models the number of successes in n independent Bernoulli trials with the same p.

reference_answer: a single success/failure trial with success probability p

question: What does the binomial distribution model?
gold_answers: the number of successes in n independent Bernoulli trials with the same p
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: The Bernoulli distribution models a single success/failure trial with success probability p. The binomial distribution models the number of successes in n independent Bernoulli trials with the same p.

reference_answer: the number of successes in n independent Bernoulli trials with the same p

question: How is conditional probability P(A given B) defined when P(B) is positive?
gold_answers: P(A and B) divided by P(B)
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: Conditional probability P(A given B) is the probability of A restricted to the information that B occurred. When P(B) is positive, P(A given B) equals P(A and B) divided by P(B).

reference_answer: P(A and B) divided by P(B)

question: In odds form, what does Bayes' theorem say about posterior odds?
gold_answers: posterior odds equal prior odds times the likelihood ratio
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: Bayes' theorem relates the posterior probability of a hypothesis given data to the prior and the likelihood. In odds form, posterior odds equal prior odds times the likelihood ratio.

reference_answer: posterior odds equal prior odds times the likelihood ratio

question: What does a prior distribution encode?
gold_answers: beliefs about a parameter before observing the current dataset
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: A prior distribution encodes beliefs about a parameter before observing the current dataset. A posterior distribution updates that belief after conditioning on the observed data.

reference_answer: beliefs about a parameter before observing the current dataset

question: What is base-rate neglect?
gold_answers: ignoring the prior frequency of a class when interpreting a diagnostic test
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: Base-rate neglect is a reasoning error that ignores the prior frequency of a class when interpreting a diagnostic test. Bayes' theorem makes the base rate an explicit input.

reference_answer: ignoring the prior frequency of a class when interpreting a diagnostic test

question: Why can a high-sensitivity, high-specificity test still have modest positive predictive value?
gold_answers: when the condition is rare
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: Medical testing examples in textbooks often show that even a high-sensitivity, high-specificity test can yield modest positive predictive value when the condition is rare.

reference_answer: when the condition is rare

question: How are marginal probabilities recovered from a joint distribution?
gold_answers: by summing or integrating out the other variable
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: Joint probability describes the simultaneous occurrence of two events or the joint distribution of two random variables. Marginal probabilities are recovered by summing or integrating out the other variable.

reference_answer: by summing or integrating out the other variable

question: What does the chain rule state for three events A, B, and C?
gold_answers: P(A and B and C) equals P(A) times P(B given A) times P(C given A and B)
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: The chain rule factors a joint probability into a product of conditional probabilities. For three events, P(A and B and C) equals P(A) times P(B given A) times P(C given A and B).

reference_answer: P(A and B and C) equals P(A) times P(B given A) times P(C given A and B)

question: What is the difference between combinations and permutations in counting?
gold_answers: combinations ignore order; permutations preserve order
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: Counting tools such as permutations and combinations support uniform probability calculations on finite spaces. Combinations ignore order; permutations preserve order.

reference_answer: combinations ignore order; permutations preserve order

question: How does Monte Carlo simulation approximate probabilities?
gold_answers: by generating many random outcomes and measuring relative frequencies
title: probability

evidence_spans.text: Simulation approximates probabilities by generating many random outcomes under a specified model and measuring relative frequencies. Monte Carlo estimates improve with more independent trials, subject to sampling variability.

reference_answer: by generating many random outcomes and measuring relative frequencies
